topic: Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic
subject: chemistry

items.q: In metallic bonding, the specification describes the particles as:
items.correct: atoms that share delocalised electrons
items.misconception: positive ions attracted to negative ions
items.why: The standard representation marks the metal particles with a positive charge, and students match that against the picture of an ionic lattice they already know. Ionic bonding requires two kinds of ion, formed by transferring electrons from one substance to another. In a metal nothing is transferred away - the outer electrons are shared by all the atoms at once, which is what the plus signs and the sea of electrons are drawn to show.
items.random_wrong: atoms that each keep their own outer electrons

items.q: Magnesium oxide is formed from magnesium and oxygen. What bonding does it contain?
items.correct: Ionic, because a metal has combined with a non-metal
items.misconception: Covalent, because two different elements have combined
items.why: Ionic bonding is usually taught first and is often introduced simply as 'what happens when two elements combine'. Students remember the outcome - a compound - without holding on to the condition that one element must be a metal. Check the periodic table before deciding. Metal plus non-metal gives ionic bonding; non-metal plus non-metal gives covalent bonding. Water and carbon dioxide are compounds, but hydrogen, oxygen and carbon are all non-metals, so both are covalent.
items.random_wrong: Metallic, because one of the elements is a metal

items.q: Which statement about covalent bonding is correct?
items.correct: It occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals
items.misconception: It occurs only in compounds, and never in elements such as oxygen
items.why: Bonding is introduced through reactions, where different elements combine. Students then attach the idea of bonding to 'compound' and think of an element as loose, unbonded atoms. Oxygen gas is O2 - two oxygen atoms sharing two pairs of electrons. Hydrogen, chlorine, nitrogen and oxygen are all non-metallic elements held together by covalent bonds.
items.random_wrong: It occurs whenever two atoms of different elements join together

items.q: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. The bonding in brass is:
items.correct: metallic, because metallic bonding occurs in alloys
items.misconception: ionic, because copper and zinc are different elements
items.why: Students associate 'two elements together' with compounds. An alloy looks like one substance, so it feels like a compound rather than a mixture. An alloy is a mixture of metals. Every atom in it is a metal atom, so all the outer electrons are delocalised and the bonding throughout is metallic.
items.random_wrong: covalent, because the two metals share outer electrons

items.q: Why is the ionic bond in sodium chloride described as strong?
items.correct: There are strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
items.misconception: The transfer of the electron from sodium to chlorine is itself the bond
items.why: The electron transfer is the dramatic, memorable step in the story, so students identify it as the bond. The attraction that follows is invisible and easy to skip. Transfer is how the ions are made; the bond is what happens next. Once sodium is Na+ and chlorine is Cl-, the opposite charges attract electrostatically, and that attraction is the ionic bond.
items.random_wrong: Pairs of electrons are shared strongly by the sodium and the chlorine

items.q: A sodium atom (2,8,1) reacts with a chlorine atom (2,8,7). What happens to the electrons?
items.correct: Sodium loses one electron and chlorine gains one electron
items.misconception: Sodium gains seven electrons to complete its outer shell
items.why: Students learn the rule 'atoms want a full outer shell' and apply it by filling the shell up, without asking which route involves moving fewer electrons or which element is the metal. The specification is explicit: electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred away. Losing one electron leaves sodium with 2,8 - the electronic structure of neon - which is a full outer shell too.
items.random_wrong: Sodium gains one electron and so becomes positively charged

items.q: An oxygen atom has the electronic structure 2,6. What is the electronic structure of the oxide ion?
items.why: Students know the identity of the element is fixed by the protons, and wrongly extend 'nothing has changed' to the electrons, which are exactly what has changed. Adjust the electron count for the charge. Mg is 2,8,2; Mg2+ has lost two electrons and is 2,8 - the structure of neon. O is 2,6; O2- has gained two and is 2,8.

items.q: An element in Group 2 of the periodic table forms an ion. What is the charge on that ion?
items.why: 'Lose' and 'negative' both feel like decrease, and students reason about the change rather than about the balance of charges left behind. Count the charges. Sodium has 11 protons and 11 electrons; lose one electron and there are 11 positives to 10 negatives, so the ion is Na+. Chlorine gains one electron, so 17 protons to 18 electrons gives Cl-.

items.q: Potassium is in Group 1 and sulfur is in Group 6. Which pair of ion charges is correct?
items.correct: K+ and S2-
items.misconception: K+ and S6-
items.why: The rule works for Groups 1 and 2, where charge equals group number, so students over-generalise it to the right-hand side of the table. For metals the charge equals the group number because those electrons are lost. For non-metals count how many electrons are needed to fill the outer shell: Group 6 needs 2, giving 2-; Group 7 needs 1, giving 1-.
items.random_wrong: K- and S2+

items.q: In a dot and cross diagram for sodium chloride, the sodium ion should be drawn showing:
items.correct: an empty outer shell, in square brackets with a + charge
items.misconception: one outer electron, in square brackets with a + charge
items.why: Students draw the two atoms first and then add an arrow, leaving the original electron in place rather than redrawing the shells after transfer. The diagram must show the situation after transfer. Sodium's outer shell is now empty, drawn as [Na]+ with 2,8 remaining, and the transferred electron appears in the chlorine as one of the eight, drawn as [Cl]- with the transferred electron marked as a cross.
items.random_wrong: one outer electron, with no brackets and no charge shown

items.q: A dot and cross diagram is drawn for magnesium chloride. What should it show?
items.correct: Two chloride ions, each with a charge of 1-
items.misconception: One chloride ion, with a charge of 2-
items.why: The one-to-one picture of sodium chloride is learned first and applied to every ionic compound without checking that the charges balance. Balance the charges to zero. One Mg2+ contributes 2+, so two Cl- ions are needed to contribute 2-. Magnesium has two outer electrons and each chlorine atom can accept only one, so two chlorine atoms are required.
items.random_wrong: Two chloride ions, each with a charge of 7-

items.q: Which statement best describes the bonding in a giant ionic lattice?
items.correct: Strong electrostatic forces act in all directions between the ions
items.misconception: Each positive ion is bonded to one negative ion beside it
items.why: The formula looks exactly like a molecular formula, and dot and cross diagrams show a single pair of ions, which reinforces the idea of a pair that belongs together. NaCl is an empirical formula - it gives the ratio, not a molecule. In the lattice each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge and attracts all of them, in all directions, so no single partner can be picked out.
items.random_wrong: Electrons transfer continuously between the ions in the lattice

items.q: A diagram shows a regular repeating array of alternating Na+ and Cl- particles. What can be deduced?
items.correct: It is ionic, because oppositely charged ions are arranged in a lattice
items.misconception: It is molecular, because each sodium is paired with one chlorine
items.why: The formula looks exactly like a molecular formula, and dot and cross diagrams show a single pair of ions, which reinforces the idea of a pair that belongs together. NaCl is an empirical formula - it gives the ratio, not a molecule. In the lattice each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge and attracts all of them, in all directions, so no single partner can be picked out.
items.random_wrong: It is covalent, because sodium and chlorine share electrons here

items.q: What is a limitation of a two-dimensional diagram of the sodium chloride lattice?
items.correct: It cannot show that the lattice extends in three dimensions
items.misconception: It shows the ions touching when they are really far apart
items.why: The model is solid, three-dimensional and used in class as though it were the thing itself, so students read it literally rather than as a deliberate simplification. State the limitation precisely: bonds are forces, not rods, and in the real structure the particles touch. The model also shows only a tiny part of what is a giant structure.
items.random_wrong: It shows the wrong ratio of sodium ions to chloride ions

items.q: What is a limitation of using a ball and stick model for a giant structure?
items.correct: It shows the particles too far apart and bonds as solid sticks
items.misconception: It shows the particles at correct spacing but only in two dimensions
items.why: The model is solid, three-dimensional and used in class as though it were the thing itself, so students read it literally rather than as a deliberate simplification. State the limitation precisely: bonds are forces, not rods, and in the real structure the particles touch. The model also shows only a tiny part of what is a giant structure.
items.random_wrong: It cannot show the ratio in which the particles are joined

items.q: A model of an ionic compound shows 4 calcium ions and 8 fluoride ions. Its empirical formula is:
items.correct: CaF2
items.misconception: Ca4F8
items.why: Students transfer the counting method used for molecular formulae, where the actual number of atoms is what is wanted, to a giant structure where only the ratio has meaning. A model of a giant structure shows only a fragment, and ions at the edges are cut off, which is why the counts are not exactly equal. Reduce the counts to the simplest whole number ratio: 1 sodium to 1 chloride, so NaCl.
items.random_wrong: Ca2F

items.q: Which statement about the covalent bonds inside a water molecule is correct?
items.correct: They are strong bonds between the atoms in the molecule
items.misconception: They are weak, because water boils at quite a low temperature
items.why: Students have one mental slot for 'the forces in this substance' and fill it from the melting point, without separating the bonds inside a molecule from the forces between molecules. Distinguish the two. The covalent bonds within the molecule are strong - the specification says so directly. What is easily overcome when a molecular substance melts is the attraction between separate molecules, not the bonds inside them.
items.random_wrong: They are formed by electrons transferring between the atoms

items.q: Which formula represents a substance that consists of small molecules?
items.correct: CO2
items.misconception: NaCl
items.why: Students judge from the appearance of the formula alone, because HCl, CO2 and NaCl all look alike written down. Look at the elements, not the length of the formula. Sodium is a metal, so NaCl is ionic; hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so HCl is a small molecule. Small molecules are made only of non-metals.
items.random_wrong: SiO2

items.q: Poly(ethene) and diamond are both covalently bonded. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Poly(ethene) has very large molecules; diamond is giant covalent
items.misconception: Both are giant covalent structures because both have many atoms
items.why: 'Very large' and 'giant' sound like the same idea, and both types have many atoms held by strong covalent bonds. The specification lists them separately. A polymer is a long chain molecule with a definite start and end; a giant covalent structure such as diamond or silicon dioxide is bonded in every direction with no separate molecules at all.
items.random_wrong: Both consist of small molecules held by weak covalent bonds

items.q: A polymer is drawn as a repeating unit inside brackets with a subscript n. The n shows that:
items.correct: the unit in the brackets is repeated a large number of times
items.misconception: the polymer molecule contains exactly n carbon atoms in total
items.why: Every other subscript in chemistry is a definite number, so a letter in the same position is read as an unknown waiting to be found. The specification simply states that n is a large number. It is not a fixed value and different molecules of the same polymer have different values of n, which is why the letter is used.
items.random_wrong: the structure inside the brackets is a giant covalent lattice

items.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the two atoms in an oxygen molecule, O2?
items.correct: Two
items.misconception: One
items.why: The first molecules met are H2, HCl, H2O and CH4, all of which have only single bonds, so students generalise from that set. Count what each atom needs. Oxygen is 2,6 and needs two more electrons, so two pairs are shared - a double bond. Nitrogen is 2,5 and needs three, so three pairs are shared - a triple bond. Each atom then has eight outer electrons.
items.random_wrong: Four

items.q: In a dot and cross diagram of ammonia, NH3, the nitrogen atom is shown with:
items.correct: three shared pairs and one pair that is not shared
items.misconception: three shared electrons and five that are not shared
items.why: Students count the dots and crosses in the overlap region individually, because the diagram shows separate marks rather than an obvious pair. Count pairs, not marks. In the overlap of a single bond there is one dot and one cross - two electrons making one bond. Oxygen shows four electrons in the overlap, which is two pairs, so a double bond.
items.random_wrong: three shared pairs and no other outer shell electrons

items.q: In a displayed formula, what does one line drawn between two atoms represent?
items.correct: One shared pair of electrons, that is a single covalent bond
items.misconception: One single electron passed from one atom to the other atom
items.why: One line looks like one thing, and the link back to the dot and cross diagram, where each bond is drawn as two electrons, is not made explicit. Convert between the two representations. Every line in a displayed formula replaces one shared pair, so methane's four lines stand for eight bonding electrons, and a double bond is drawn as two lines.
items.random_wrong: The transfer of an electron from one atom to another atom

items.q: A ball and stick model shows one black ball joined by four sticks to four white balls. Black is carbon and white is hydrogen. The molecular formula is:
items.correct: CH4
items.misconception: C4H4
items.why: Students count everything visible in the model rather than deciding first which parts represent atoms and which represent bonds. Identify the elements from the key, then count only the balls. A model with one black ball and four white balls is CH4 - the four sticks are the four covalent bonds, not extra atoms.
items.random_wrong: CH

items.q: Why are the outer electrons in a metal able to move through the whole structure?
items.correct: They are delocalised, so they are not held by any one atom
items.misconception: They are held loosely in the outer shell of their own atom
items.why: Every earlier model of the atom fixes electrons in shells around one nucleus, and 'delocalised' is a new word that is easy to say without changing that picture. Delocalised means no longer associated with any one atom. The outer electrons form a sea spread through the whole giant structure, and it is the sharing of these delocalised electrons that gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
items.random_wrong: They are attracted to the negative ions within the lattice

items.q: Which phrase describes the structure of a pure metal?
items.correct: A giant structure of atoms arranged in a regular pattern
items.misconception: A giant structure of atoms joined by shared pairs of electrons
items.why: The word 'share' appears in two of the three definitions, and students blur transfer and sharing because both end with full outer shells. Match the word to the bond: ionic - transfer, giving oppositely charged ions; covalent - atoms share pairs of electrons; metallic - atoms share delocalised electrons. In sodium chloride the electron leaves sodium completely and stays on chlorine.
items.random_wrong: A lattice of positive and negative ions attracting each other

items.q: Is silicon dioxide made of SiO2 molecules?
items.correct: No. Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure, and SiO2 is its empirical formula.
items.misconception: SiO2 looks just like CO2, so silicon dioxide must be made of small molecules in the same way.
items.why: The two formulae are written identically, and students take the formula as evidence of a molecule without asking whether the substance is molecular or giant. Learn the specification's examples: diamond and silicon dioxide are the named giant covalent structures. In silicon dioxide every silicon atom is covalently bonded to oxygen atoms throughout the structure, so SiO2 gives the ratio, not a molecule.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a covalent bond act in all directions like an ionic bond?
items.correct: No. In an ionic lattice the electrostatic forces act in all directions; a covalent bond is a shared pair between two particular atoms.
items.misconception: All strong bonds work the same way, so the atoms in a molecule attract every other atom around them equally.
items.why: The phrase 'act in all directions' is memorised as a general fact about bonding rather than as the specific feature of an ionic lattice that the specification states. Keep the phrase where it belongs. It describes ionic bonding in the lattice. A covalent bond involves a shared pair of electrons between two named atoms, which is why molecules have definite shapes and definite formulae.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should a molecular formula be simplified to its lowest ratio?
items.correct: No. A molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element in the molecule.
items.misconception: Formulae should always be written in the simplest form, so a model of ethene, C2H4, should be written as CH2.
items.why: Empirical formulae are practised for ionic compounds just before this, and students carry the habit of simplifying across to molecules. Match the method to the question. For a giant ionic structure work out the simplest ratio; for a molecule count the atoms and leave the numbers alone. C2H4 is the molecular formula of ethene and must not be reduced.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.2.1 Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic
